43.title: The sheet of flowers, 1539
43.hook: tradition says that when Nanak died, Hindus and Muslims both claimed his body, and under the sheet they found only flowers
43.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's passing, traditionally dated 1539 at Kartarpur, where Gurdwara Darbar Sahib keeps both a samadh and a grave; the story of the flowers is told as a sign that he belonged to all people.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tests of Lehna, and wet grass on fine clothes. Just do it well.

A funeral is about who a person was. It can also turn into a quarrel over who gets to say goodbye, and how. Kartarpur, 1539, by tradition's date. Guru Nanak is old now, and he's dying. Word spreads through the villages, and people come: Hindus who had followed him, and Muslims who had followed him. As they gather, a hard question rises. Hindus cremate their dead. Muslims bury theirs. So when the Guru is gone, which will it be? Who does he belong to?
screen: `WHO GETS TO SAY GOODBYE?` → `KARTARPUR, 1539.` → `HINDUS CREMATE. MUSLIMS BURY.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak heard the argument and settled it before it could start. Bring flowers, he said. Hindus, lay yours on my right side. Muslims, lay yours on my left. Whichever flowers are still fresh in the morning, that side may do as it wishes. Then he drew a sheet over himself, and died. In the morning his followers lifted the sheet. The body was gone. There were only the flowers, on both sides, and both were fresh. So, the story says, they cut the sheet in two. The Hindus cremated their half. The Muslims buried theirs. At Kartarpur today, there is a memorial and a grave, side by side. Sikhs hear this story in different ways. For some it's a miracle, a last sign. For others it's a picture of what the whole life meant. Either way, look at its shape. Remember his first words after the river: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. He didn't say that to erase anyone. Both groups kept their own ways; both grieved as their tradition taught. What he refused was to be owned by one side against the other. Even at the very end, he gave both sides something. Flowers for everyone. That's where Guru Nanak's story closes, twenty-two days of it: a boy at Talwandi, the river, the rebab, the road, Kartarpur. But he didn't leave the community without a leader. Before he died, he had already chosen who would carry the light, and given him a new name.

segments.voice: Hold a flower, or a leaf or a picture if there's none handy, and think of where you'd lay it: a desk at work, a grave you haven't visited, the doorstep of a neighbor you don't know well, a shared kitchen. Let it be for someone whose goodness belongs to more than one group of people.
Phull. Flowers, the word behind the sheet Guru Nanak asked Hindus and Muslims to lay flowers on at his death, both halves found fresh by morning.
Your line: flowers for everyone. Tomorrow, the trader with the wet grass becomes Angad. That's day forty-three.

44.title: Lehna becomes Angad
44.hook: Nanak names Lehna his successor and calls him Angad, part of my own body
44.howItsDone: Sikhs understand the ten Gurus as one light passing through ten bodies, and they refer to the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib as angs, limbs of the Guru; Guru Angad's accession is remembered each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sheet of flowers, phull, and a Guru who belonged to no one side. Flowers for everyone.

Guru Nanak had two grown sons. The elder, Sri Chand, was deeply devout, an ascetic who had renounced ordinary life. The younger, Lakhmi Das, was a householder with a family. When a founder steps down, the next in line can seem obvious, the way the eldest son takes over the family shop. Either son would have been the obvious choice. But for years Nanak had been watching someone else: the trader who carried the wet grass, cleared the ditch and fished the bowl out of dirty water. So step back a little in time, to a few months before the flowers, and the day Nanak made his choice.
screen: `EVERYONE ASSUMES THE SON.` → `TWO SONS, BOTH DEVOUT.` → `THE GURU WAS WATCHING SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak placed a coconut and five copper coins before Lehna and bowed to him. The teacher bowed to the student. Then he gave him a new name: Angad. Today's word is inside it. Ang means a limb, a part of the body, so Angad is often explained as part of my own body. This man isn't my replacement, the Guru was saying; he's me, continued. A ballad in the scripture, sung by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, says it plainly: the light was the same, the way was the same; the king had only changed his body. That's the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus. Not ten teachers with ten different messages, but one light passed from one body to the next, like a flame lit from a flame. That's why the Gurus whose hymns are in the scripture signed them not with their own names but with Nanak's. The word takes one more turn. Ang also names the pages of the Sikh scripture. You don't say page 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib; you say Ang 360. Each page is a limb of the Guru. The word that named the second Guru now names every page of the book Sikhs call their Guru today. And notice: Nanak didn't choose by blood. He chose the one who had become a servant. The light went to the one who could carry it, and it's still traveling.

segments.voice: Think of something you care about: a skill, a family recipe, a way of doing your job, a value your parents gave you. Then see the face of whoever might carry it after you, a child, a colleague, a friend, a student. If nobody comes to mind, notice that too, and wonder who it might be.
Ang. A limb, a part of the body; inside the name Angad, and the word Sikhs use for every page of their scripture. Today's word.

45.title: The Guru's script
45.hook: at Khadur, Guru Angad shapes and teaches the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people can read the hymns
45.howItsDone: Sikh children often learn Gurmukhi at home or in gurdwara classes so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves; any Sikh, of any gender or caste, may read from the scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ang, a limb, and the name Angad, part of my own body. Passing the light.

Remember the first time you read something on your own? A cereal box, a street sign, a picture book. Something clicked, and a world that had belonged to grown-ups belonged to you too. For most people in the Punjab of the 1500s, that click never came. Reading was for priests, scholars and clerks. Sacred texts were in Sanskrit, Arabic or Persian, languages ordinary farmers didn't speak, in scripts they couldn't read. Guru Nanak's hymns, sung in the people's own language, were passed along by memory and in rough notes. Then the new Guru, Angad, moved to a village called Khadur, and there, tradition says, he sat down with the children.
screen: `THE FIRST TIME YOU READ ALONE.` → `READING WAS FOR THE FEW.` → `GURU ANGAD SITS WITH THE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The script is called Gurmukhi. Guru is the teacher and mukh is the mouth, so Gurmukhi is often explained as from the mouth of the Guru. The Sikh scripture is written in it, and so is Punjabi across India today. One careful note: Guru Angad didn't invent writing out of nothing. Scripts much like it were already used in the Punjab, especially by traders keeping accounts. What Sikh tradition credits him with is shaping those letters into a clear, standard alphabet, putting them in order and teaching them, so anyone could learn to read the Guru's words. Tradition says he taught the letters to children himself, and helped put together an early primer. On many paths, the holy words sat in a language only specialists could read, so ordinary people needed someone in between. Guru Angad did the opposite: the hymns in the people's own language, in letters a farmer's child could learn, so the word could go straight from the page into anyone's life. That's a big part of why Sikhs still treat reading the scripture as something for everyone, man or woman, of any caste. No priestly class holds the book. Anyone who can read Gurmukhi can read the Guru. Even the first symbol you learned, Ik Onkar, the numeral one and its curve, is written in these letters.

segments.voice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper, and write your name one letter at a time, slower than you ever do, watching each shape form. Somebody taught you these letters once; maybe you remember who, a parent at a kitchen table, a teacher in a classroom. Let your pen move slowly enough to remember them.
Gurmukhi. The script Guru Angad shaped and taught at Khadur, from the mouth of the Guru, so ordinary people could read the hymns themselves.

46.title: Mata Khivi's kitchen
46.hook: Guru Angad's wife runs the langar and is remembered for serving rich rice pudding to all
46.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Mata Khivi as a shaper of the langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve anyone who comes, seated together; kheer is still often served there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gurmukhi, the Guru's script, shaped so anyone could read. Letters for everyone.

Some of a family's deepest teaching happens in the kitchen, nowhere near a classroom or a place of worship. Who gets fed first. Whether there's always room for one more. What you do when someone shows up hungry and unannounced. At Khadur, while Guru Angad taught the letters, another teacher was at work, and her classroom was a kitchen. Her name was Mata Khivi. Mata means mother, a title of respect. She was Guru Angad's wife, and she ran the langar, the free community kitchen where everyone who came was fed, sitting side by side. Today, what she served, and what it taught.
screen: `THE KITCHEN TABLE TEACHES.` → `MATA KHIVI, GURU ANGAD'S WIFE.` → `SHE RAN THE LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Mata Khivi is in the scripture. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a ballad by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, says, in paraphrase, that Khivi is a good woman who gives cool, leafy shade to everyone, like a great tree. In her kitchen, it says, the Guru's bounty is shared out, and the kheer, rice pudding rich with ghee, the clarified butter, tastes like nectar. A book of hymns about God honors a woman for her cooking and her kindness. That's not a small thing. It says the kitchen is holy ground too. Why rice pudding? In that time and place, kheer made with ghee was a rich food, the kind served at celebrations or to honored guests, not handed out to whoever walked in. Mata Khivi served the good stuff to everyone, the laborer and the landlord at the same meal. Remember Lalo's bread? That was honest food earned by hard work. This is the other side of the same teaching: when you share, share the best you have. Sikh tradition remembers Mata Khivi as one of the people who made the langar what it is today, not just a charity meal but a table where everyone is an honored guest. A gurdwara kitchen stirring a pot of dal for strangers tonight is, in some way, still her kitchen.

segments.voice: Think of someone you could give a sweet thing: a coworker, a neighbor, the person who delivers your mail, someone at home. Not the leftover cookie; the good one, and picture their face as you hand it over. If you can't give food, give something else sweet: a real compliment, a thank-you note.
Kheer. The rich rice pudding Mata Khivi served to everyone in the langar at Khadur, and for which she is honored by name in the scripture.

47.title: The wrestling ground
47.hook: Guru Angad encourages exercise and wrestling so body and spirit grow strong together
47.tomorrow: an old man hears a hymn
47.howItsDone: Sikh tradition values physical health and strength alongside prayer; gurdwaras sometimes host sports, and martial arts such as gatka are practiced in Sikh communities, with Khadur Sahib's Mall Akhara remembered as Guru Angad's wrestling ground.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kheer, Mata Khivi's rich rice pudding, served to everyone. The kitchen is a teacher.

There's an old idea, in a lot of places, that the spiritual life happens from the neck up. The body just carries your soul around, and maybe gets in the way. So holy people are pictured thin, pale and still. Khadur, in Guru Angad's day, looked different. In the mornings, hymns. At midday, the kitchen, with Mata Khivi's pudding. And in the evenings, tradition says, a patch of packed earth where young men stripped to the waist and wrestled, while the Guru himself watched and cheered them on.
screen: `SPIRITUAL FROM THE NECK UP?` → `KHADUR, IN GURU ANGAD'S DAY.` → `PACKED EARTH, AND WRESTLERS.`

segments.voice: That patch of earth is an akhara: a wrestling ground, a training place. Across South Asia, wrestling was an old and serious art, with its own teachers, its own discipline and its own pits of soft earth. Sikh tradition says Guru Angad set up an akhara at Khadur, and a gurdwara there is still named for it: the Mall Akhara, the wrestlers' ground. He encouraged young people to exercise, to wrestle, to be strong and healthy. Why would a Guru care about push-ups? Because on this path, the body isn't the enemy. Guru Nanak had told the yogis on the mountain that you don't need to leave the world to find God; you live in it, unstained. And living in the world takes a body that can work a field, carry water, stand up for a neighbor. Health isn't vanity; it's part of being useful. The picture shows up in the scripture too. In a hymn by the fifth Guru, Arjan, the speaker calls himself a wrestler, a champion of the Lord, come into the arena of the world. Life itself is the akhara, and Sikhs read the real opponents as inner ones, like ego, greed and anger. So the ground at Khadur was both things at once: a real place to train the body, and a picture of the struggle inside. Later Gurus would build on this, in harder times, but that story comes later.
screen: `AKHARA — A WRESTLING GROUND.` · `THE BODY ISN'T THE ENEMY.` · `STRONG ENOUGH TO BE USEFUL.` · `LIFE ITSELF IS THE ARENA.` · then, large: `THE BODY COUNTS TOO.`

segments.voice: For three minutes, stand if you can: roll your shoulders, stretch your arms up, fold forward, then march in place, do a few squats or walk around the room. If you can't stand, move what you can: hands, neck, breath. Don't make it a workout; make it a thank-you to the body that carries you.
Akhara. A wrestling ground; at Khadur, a place where Guru Angad had young people train their bodies alongside their spirits. Today's word.
Your line: the body counts too. Tomorrow, an old man hears a hymn. Nice work today.

48.title: An old man hears a hymn
48.hook: past sixty, Amar Das hears Guru Angad's daughter Bibi Amro singing Nanak's words at dawn, and goes to find the Guru
48.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das as the third Guru and tell of Bibi Amro's singing as the moment that brought him to Guru Angad; Sikh daily practice begins with the Gurus' hymns in the early morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the akhara, the wrestling ground at Khadur. The body counts too.

A song drifts out of an open window, and a passerby stops walking. He didn't choose it; it found him. This passerby has been looking his whole life. His name is Amar Das. Tradition says he's past sixty, a respected man in his village, deeply devout, and that he has walked to the Ganges on pilgrimage again and again. He's done everything a devout man is supposed to do, and he still feels something missing. His nephew has married a young woman named Bibi Amro, who happens to be Guru Angad's daughter. And one morning before dawn, Amar Das hears her singing while she works.
screen: `A SONG FROM AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `AMAR DAS, PAST SIXTY, STILL LOOKING.` → `BIBI AMRO SINGS AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: She was singing a hymn of Guru Nanak's. Tradition doesn't agree on exactly which one, but the effect is the same in every telling. Amar Das stood still and listened, then asked her: whose words are those? My father's teacher, she said, Guru Nanak. And my father, Guru Angad, carries his light now, at Khadur. So an old man of standing got up and went to find a teacher much younger than himself. He bowed at Guru Angad's feet, and stayed. He would become the third Guru, but not for many years. Notice three things. First, who carried the hymn: not a priest or a scholar, but a young woman singing while she did her morning work. The word traveled the way it was meant to, through ordinary people's voices, in their own language. That's what Guru Angad's letters and Mardana's rebab were for. Second, what the hymns are on this path. Sikhs call the Gurus' words bani, and they treat bani itself as a teacher, as alive. A hymn heard at the right moment can change a whole life. Third, age. Amar Das had every reason to think his path was settled. He'd done the pilgrimages. He was old. Instead he started again as a beginner, and spent long years learning to serve before anyone called him Guru. Sikhs tell his story to say the door is open at any age, and it's never too late to hear something new.

Bani. The Gurus' hymns, treated by Sikhs as a living teacher, one of which stopped Amar Das, past sixty, as Bibi Amro sang it at dawn.

49.title: The water carrier
49.hook: for years he carries water for Guru Angad before dawn; tradition says he stumbled by a weaver's peg and was mocked as homeless
49.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water as a model of seva, humble service; Guru Angad's reply to the weaver's wife is often recited in the story, and Sikhs often volunteer in small, unseen tasks at the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bani, the hymn that turned Amar Das into a beginner again. It's never too late. Today closes a week.

Every morning, long before sunrise, Amar Das, the old man who'd come to Khadur, walked to the river Beas, filled a pitcher with water, and carried it back for Guru Angad's bath. A long walk, there and back, in the dark, every day, in every season. Tradition says he did it for twelve years. It's the kind of job some people do faithfully for years: the crossing guard there every morning in the rain, the neighbor who's brought in your trash cans since you moved in, the parent who packs the lunch every school day. Nobody writes songs about them. Today, one stormy night on that road.
screen: `TO THE RIVER AND BACK, BEFORE DAWN.` → `TWELVE YEARS, TRADITION SAYS.` → `THE SAME SMALL JOB, FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: It was dark and pouring rain, tradition says, and the old man was coming back with the full pitcher. Near a weaver's house he tripped over a peg in the ground, one of the stakes weavers use to stretch their thread, and fell. He didn't spill the water. But the noise woke the weaver, who asked who was out there at that hour. His wife answered, scornfully: it must be Amru, the homeless one, who has no place of his own and hangs around the Guru for scraps. Amar Das didn't argue. He picked himself up and carried the water home. When the story reached Guru Angad, tradition says, he answered with a list of honors: Amar Das is the home of the homeless, the honor of those with no honor, the strength of those with none. Not long after, he named Amar Das the third Guru. Sikhs keep telling this because it turns the insult inside out. The one mocked as having no place becomes the one who gives everyone a place. Now look back at the week. The sheet of flowers, for everyone. Lehna becomes Angad, part of the Guru's own body. The Guru's script, letters for everyone. Mata Khivi's kitchen. The wrestling ground. An old man who heard a hymn. And a water carrier on a dark road. Again and again, people were chosen, or remembered, for faithfulness when nobody was watching. Guru Angad's light passed to the man who carried the water.
screen: `A WEAVER'S PEG, IN THE RAIN.` · `AMRU, THE HOMELESS ONE.` · `THE HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · `THE WEEK: FAITHFUL, UNWATCHED.` · then, large: `FAITHFUL IN SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you do for someone that nobody notices: filling the water jug, taking out the recycling, checking on an elderly neighbor. Picture doing it a little more carefully than usual, without mentioning it to anyone. If someone mocks it, or ignores it, let it go; just carry the water.
Seva. Selfless service, the heart of the years Amar Das spent carrying water before dawn for Guru Angad, mocked as homeless, and named the home of the homeless.
Your line: faithful in small things. Tomorrow, a well of eighty-four steps. That's seven full weeks.
